title: Breadth-first search: exploring in rings
objectives: Explain why BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs
Follow the queue as BFS explores

sections.title: The way out of a maze

blocks.markdown:
Drop ink at the start of a maze and it spreads one cell at a time in every direction. The first moment the ink touches the exit, it has found a shortest route.

Breadth-first search works the same way: it explores everything 1 step away, then 2 steps, then 3.

blocks.question: In the maze below, moving up, down, left or right, how many moves is the shortest path from S to G?
blocks.explanation: The only way across is the gap in the middle row, then up and around the right-hand wall: 14 moves.

steps.title: Start at A
steps.narration: The queue holds the frontier: nodes found but not yet explored. It starts with A.

steps.title: Explore A
steps.narration: Take A from the front and add its neighbours B and C to the back: both are 1 step away.

steps.title: Explore B
steps.narration: B's new neighbour is D, 2 steps from A. It goes behind C.

steps.title: Explore C
steps.narration: C reaches D, already queued, and E, which is new.

steps.title: Explore D
steps.narration: D finds F, 3 steps from A. Every node 2 steps away came out of the queue before it.

steps.title: Explore E
steps.narration: E's neighbours are all known, so nothing is added.

steps.title: Explore F
steps.narration: The queue empties: every node was reached in order of distance, A, B, C, D, E, F.

blocks.question: Which data structure holds BFS's frontier?
blocks.explanation: A queue is first in, first out, so nodes leave in the order they were found: nearest first. A stack would give depth-first search.

blocks.question: Why does BFS find a shortest path in an unweighted maze?
options: It reaches cells in order of their distance from the start
It always moves towards the goal
It tries every path and keeps the shortest
It remembers the last turn it took
blocks.explanation: Every cell at distance k is reached before any cell at distance k + 1, so the first time BFS reaches the goal, no shorter path is left.

rows.label: Memory
cells: A whole ring of the frontier

blocks.question: You need the fewest friend-of-a-friend hops between two people. Which search fits?
blocks.explanation: Hops are unweighted steps, and BFS finds the fewest. DFS can wander down a long path first.

cards.front: What data structure does BFS use for its frontier?
cards.back: A queue: first in, first out.

cards.front: Why does BFS find shortest paths in unweighted graphs?
cards.back: It reaches nodes in order of distance from the start, so the first time it reaches the goal is via a shortest path.

cards.front: How does BFS avoid visiting a node twice?
cards.back: It marks nodes as seen when they are queued and skips neighbours already seen.

cards.front: Which search finds shortest paths when edges have different weights?
cards.back: Dijkstra's algorithm (for non-negative weights), not plain BFS.
